tEn: A Month After Going Viral: Jev's Creator on Coding Agents, Benchmarks & AI's Reliability Gap
tZh: 爆红一个月后：Jev 创作者谈编程智能体、基准测试与 AI 可靠性鸿沟
sEn: Diogo, CEO of Typescape, reflects on Jev's viral launch, the reliability gap in AI models, and what it takes to build machine-native intelligence.
sZh: Typescape CEO Diogo 回顾 Jev 爆红一个月后的思考，探讨 AI 模型的可靠性鸿沟，以及打造机器原生智能所需的条件。

consensus.en: AI is smart but not reliable; reliability, not benchmark scores, is the real bottleneck.
consensus.zh: AI 很聪明但不可靠；真正的瓶颈是可靠性，而非基准分数。

consensus.en: Models should be provider-agnostic like SQL; locking into one model's quirks is bad for developers.
consensus.zh: 模型应像 SQL 一样提供商无关；锁定某家模型的怪癖对开发者不利。

consensus.en: Multimodality degrades intelligence; text tasks will be automated before image tasks.
consensus.zh: 多模态会降低智能；文本任务将先于图像任务被自动化。

consensus.en: Coding agents give 20-40% speedup on average, but vary wildly by use case and skill.
consensus.zh: 编码智能体平均提速 20-40%，但因用例和技能差异巨大。

consensus.en: AI safety is not monolithic; ASI, biorisk, and cyber risk are distinct threat models.
consensus.zh: AI 安全并非铁板一块；超级智能、生物风险和网络风险是不同的威胁模型。

consensus.en: We are breakthroughs away from true agency; current models lack real autonomy.
consensus.zh: 我们距离真正的自主性还有多个突破；当前模型缺乏真正的自主性。

contrarian.en: Benchmarks are misleading; overpromising underdelivering burns developer goodwill and hurts the field.
contrarian.zh: 基准测试具有误导性；过度承诺和交付不足会消耗开发者善意并伤害领域。

contrarian.en: The KV cache tyranny limits coding agent design; we need architectures free from append-only state.
contrarian.zh: KV 缓存的暴政限制了编码智能体设计；我们需要摆脱仅追加状态的架构。

contrarian.en: Most people overuse chatbots and coding agents; many tasks are better served by simpler software.
contrarian.zh: 大多数人过度使用聊天机器人和编码智能体；许多任务用更简单的软件更好。

contrarian.en: Anthropic's valuation may be miscalibrated due to misunderstandings of AI's future capabilities.
contrarian.zh: 由于对 AI 未来能力的误解，Anthropic 的估值可能校准失当。

contrarian.en: The AI safety community focused on ASI is often divorced from the technology's reality.
contrarian.zh: 关注超级智能的 AI 安全社区常常脱离技术现实。

contrarian.en: Financial engineering, not models or product, is the labs' greatest strength.
contrarian.zh: 实验室最大的优势是金融工程，而非模型或产品。

turns.en: As you think about Anthropic, is that something you're optimistic on, like, hey, that's undervalued, or something where you're like, ooh, I don't know what's going to happen to that?
turns.zh: 说到 Anthropic，你是持乐观态度，觉得“嘿，这被低估了”，还是觉得“呃，我不知道它会怎么样”？

turns.en: I get the sense that a lot of the expectations baked in are ones that are not just product level, but based on misunderstandings of the future of AI and what it can do. So my guess is that because some people might be valuing it like building God is basically infinite, there will be some amount of miscalibration there. And I think that, you know, like the “let them cure cancer” is going to be like Marie Antoinette's “let them eat cake.”
turns.zh: 我感觉，很多已经计入价格的预期不只是产品层面的，而是建立在对 AI 未来及其能力的误解之上。所以我猜，因为有些人把它估值成“造神基本上就是无限价值”，那里会有一定程度的错配。而且我觉得，“让他们去治愈癌症”这句话会变得像玛丽·安托瓦内特的“让他们吃蛋糕”一样。

turns.en: Jev took the AI world by storm about a month ago, and I've been wanting to talk to Jo, their CEO of Typescape, for quite some time. So it was really fun to have him on the podcast. I think maybe even better with a month to reflect on everything that's happened, because we talked about a ton of different things. It was really awesome to get Jo's perspective on the shapes of problems that he still thinks need to be solved by AI models, how he thinks about pushing Jev models to be even better. It was also fun to get his thoughts on Anthropic's upcoming IPO, AI safety, a bunch of other topics. I think folks will really enjoy hearing from him. Without further ado, here's Jo.
turns.zh: 大约一个月前，Jev 席卷了整个 AI 圈，而我一直想和 Typescape 的 CEO Jo 聊聊，已经想了很久。所以能请他来播客真的很开心。我觉得隔了一个月再回顾这一切，可能还更好，因为我们聊了一大堆不同的话题。能听到 Jo 的看法真的很棒——他认为 AI 模型还需要解决哪些形态的问题，他如何思考把 Jev 模型推得更好。听他谈 Anthropic 即将到来的 IPO、AI 安全，还有一堆其他话题，也很有意思。我觉得大家会很喜欢听他讲。废话不多说，有请 Jo。

turns.en: Well, I have really been looking forward to this. I think ever since your viral launch, I feel like the second that happened, I was like, I have to have you on the podcast. And so appreciate you making this happen. I think actually in many ways even more interesting that we're some weeks removed from it, given that the early results were not what you expected and maybe not as strong as you were hoping. Like what gave you that kind of early confidence in this research direction of RLCD? I mean, I feel like you kind of alluded to it in the GPT-3 example. It seems like there has to be a leap of faith that any great research effort undergoes. And what was it about this approach that, in the early days when you didn't have the signals early on, you were still kind of confident in?
turns.zh: 我真的非常期待这次对话。我觉得自从你们那次爆火的发布之后，那一刻我就想，我必须请你上播客。非常感谢你促成这件事。其实我觉得，隔了几周再来聊，在很多方面反而更有意思，因为早期结果并不是你预期的，也许没有你希望的那么强。那么，是什么让你对 RLCD 这个研究方向有那种早期的信心？我感觉你在 GPT-3 那个例子里也隐约提到过。看起来任何伟大的研究工作都必须经历一次信念之跃。在早期还没有信号的时候，这个方法的什么特质让你依然有信心？

turns.en: Oh man, oh man, oh man. This is like, I'm getting a little emotional right now. Um, I have a fun little side topic that gets into this if that's okay. My co-founder was debating on whether or not I was mission-driven at OpenAI. I would have described myself in hindsight as one of the lowest percentile mission-driven, because I think that the OpenAI mission is not really—it's kind of intentionally left as vague so many people's missions can fit into it. But like the grand mission was never something I super believed in, even though I truly want AI to be extremely, extremely transformative. So I'm still trying to figure out, like, am I—was I mission-driven then or not? Because I'm really mission-driven now. But the answer was, you know, just a lot of work trying to square AI being super incredibly awesome, which I think it is, and AI being really not that useful in every like productivity stat around. And this is like the kind of thing that most people just focus on one or the other and they never have like a bridge answer, or like they never have a sensible bridge answer.
turns.zh: 天哪，天哪，天哪。这真是——我现在有点激动了。呃，如果你们不介意，我有个有趣的小插曲可以聊到这个。我的联合创始人在争论我在 OpenAI 时到底算不算使命驱动。事后看，我会把自己描述为使命驱动程度最低的那一档，因为我觉得 OpenAI 的使命其实并不是——它有点被故意留得模糊，好让很多人的使命都能套进去。但那个宏大的使命从来不是我特别相信的东西，尽管我真的希望 AI 变得极其、极其有变革性。所以我还在琢磨，我那时到底算不算使命驱动？因为我现在真的很有使命感。但答案是，大量的工作都在试图调和两件事：AI 超级棒（我认为确实如此），以及 AI 在周围所有生产力统计里其实没那么有用。而这类事情，大多数人只关注其中一边，从来不会有桥梁式的答案，或者说从来不会有合理的桥梁式答案。

turns.en: I think distribution is like a nonsensical answer here, because so many companies have gone all in on that and then gotten burned. It's almost certainly not distribution. And to me it was like believing that, hey, AI is clearly smart, and also that the future is clearly going to be machine-native. The question that always motivated me—and I used to ask this question even to early people joining, or even to investors in our early rounds, or even like the pre-seed round, which I don't even know if that counts, like taking a SAFE—I used to ask this question of, like, okay, imagine LLMs are an API, like a submodule that is called by software, which even in the most strong-model ends, they still need to be called by software, by something like a harness. That harness can be a while loop. But what percentage of those calls going into the LLMs are actually meant for human consumption—so for consumption, so things like style matter and pros and all of that—versus for computer consumption, which is going to be very, very different? You know, like I don't think a computer really ever wants a string, except when that string happens to be an extreme cardinality enum, which is a very valid use case. But it's very rare that that is the thing that computers want, because they operate on bits. And when I just ask myself or anyone this question, even the most strong-pilled of people will give many nines of percent for the machine-native component. It's just a question of when that will happen. And to me it was always like, okay, what does that thing look like? Let's work backwards from that cognitive core and make it work. And I will say Jev is not yet there. There's still so much more work to do to make it so much better. And that's what really drives us all.
turns.zh: 我觉得“分发”在这里是个没意义的答案，因为太多公司全力押注它，然后被烧伤了。几乎可以肯定不是分发。对我来说，是相信：嘿，AI 显然很聪明，而且未来显然会是机器原生的。一直驱动我的问题是——我以前甚至问过早期加入的人，或者我们早期几轮的投资者，甚至 pre-seed 轮（我都不知道那算不算，比如签个 SAFE）——我以前会问这个问题：好，想象 LLM 是一个 API，一个被软件调用的子模块，即使在最强模型那一端，它们仍然需要被软件调用，被某种 harness 调用。那个 harness 可以是个 while 循环。但那些进入 LLM 的调用里，有多大比例实际上是给人类消费的——为了消费，所以风格重要、韵律重要等等——对比给计算机消费的，那会非常非常不同？你知道，我不认为计算机真的想要字符串，除非那个字符串恰好是个极端基数的枚举，那是个非常有效的用例。但计算机想要那种东西的情况非常罕见，因为它们基于比特运作。而当我问自己或任何人这个问题时，即使是最“强模型至上”的人，也会给机器原生部分很多个九的百分比。只是时间问题。对我来说，一直是：好，那东西长什么样？让我们从那个认知核心倒推，把它做出来。我要说，Jev 还没到那一步。还有太多工作要做，让它变得好得多。而这正是真正驱动我们所有人的东西。

transcript.sec: Co-evolving use cases with the model

turns.en: Is Jev not yet there because—I mean, you know, today the shape of calls and tokens actually is more for humans than it is for computers themselves. How much of it is just you're also waiting for the use cases themselves to evolve, and how much of it is areas you want to push on the model?
turns.zh: Jev 还没到那一步，是因为——我是说，你知道，今天调用和 token 的形态实际上更多是给人类的，而不是给计算机本身的。这其中有多少只是你也在等待用例本身演化，又有多少是你想在模型上推进的领域？

turns.en: I think it's a bit of both. It's like this interactive dance, and this is also why we released these dreamer-ready features, like the things that we wouldn't recommend for the most stable of use cases, because we really want to be honest about our model's properties. So we've released a lot of these things because the reality is that the people who best know how much reliability, robustness, intelligence is needed for their downstream application is not us. It's the developers themselves, because developers are the expert at this and they will know way better than anyone on our team. We have smart people, but they will know better what reliability profile they need, as long as we give them the right knobs, which strong models don't tend to do. So there's like an entire spectrum of this. I think that they need to co-evolve together.
turns.zh: 我觉得两者都有。这就像一场互动舞蹈，这也是为什么我们发布了这些 dreamer-ready 功能——那些我们不会推荐用于最稳定用例的东西，因为我们真的想对模型的特性保持诚实。我们发布了很多这类东西，因为现实是，最清楚自己下游应用需要多少可靠性、鲁棒性、智能的人不是我们，而是开发者自己，因为开发者才是这方面的专家，他们比我们团队任何人都清楚得多。我们有聪明的人，但只要给对旋钮，开发者会更清楚他们需要什么样的可靠性画像，而强模型往往不这么做。所以这整个是个谱系。我认为它们需要共同演化。

turns.en: The reason why we launched was not like, okay, this is like a good moment in AI. Everyone told us not to launch then, just FYI. It was that we felt like, hey, this is getting to be something we're really proud of. Like, it's kind of impressively smart at a lot of things if you prompt it right. And we are ready to keep pushing those limits with the rest of the field to help us co-evolve use cases, figure out weaknesses, deal with jaggedness.
turns.zh: 我们发布的原因并不是“好，这是 AI 的一个好时机”。顺便说一句，当时所有人都告诉我们别在那时发布。而是我们觉得，嘿，这正在变成一件我们真正引以为傲的东西。如果你提示得当，它在很多事情上聪明得令人印象深刻。我们准备好和这个领域的其他人一起继续推进那些极限，帮助我们共同演化用例、找出弱点、应对锯齿状的能力分布。

transcript.sec: Why launch despite the doom vibe

turns.en: There's so much we do to focus on jaggedness and insufficiency and intelligence that having people play with it would be so helpful. Why did folks tell you not to launch?
turns.zh: 我们在关注模型的参差不齐、能力不足和智能水平上做了那么多工作，让大家亲自上手玩一玩会非常有帮助。为什么有人劝你别发布？

turns.en: We launched around the time of the pacing the frontier discussion, and people were like, "Hey, it's kind of a bad vibe to launch a capabilities product during this." Everyone's really doom and gloom about AI, it's kind of a bad vibe, and I don't know if you guys should do this. And we're just like, that discussion never really made sense in the first place. Or it is at best incomplete, in my opinion.
turns.zh: 我们发布的时候，正好赶上“控制前沿发展节奏”那场讨论，大家就说：“嘿，在这种时候发布一个能力型产品，氛围不太对。”所有人对 AI 都特别悲观，气氛很压抑，不知道你们该不该这么做。而我们的想法是，那场讨论从一开始就说不通。至少在我看来，它是不完整的。

turns.en: You talk about wanting to push in so many directions. One thing you guys do is you're always transparent about the things the models can't do, the areas where they're not as strong. How much of that is the roadmap for what you're pushing on, and how much is other areas? How do you think about where you want the company to push in the next month or two?
turns.zh: 你说想在很多方向上推进。你们做的一件事是，总是很坦诚地讲模型做不到什么、在哪些方面不够强。这其中有多少是你们推进的路线图，又有多少是其他领域？你怎么考虑公司接下来一两个月要在哪些方向发力？

turns.en: Month or two? Oh, that's an AI world. I don't know if I can ask longer than that, right?
turns.zh: 一两个月？哦，那是 AI 世界的时间尺度。我不知道我能不能问得比这更长，对吧？

turns.en: I wouldn't say jaggedness is purely our roadmap. There are some things that models truly are weak at, and this is where that taste stuff comes in, right? Like what I was talking about, the reality of what you can extract from these models. The reason we call them system one models, among other things — and actually people did not want us to name it that either, because system one thinking tends to be a bad thing, people use that as kind of an insult, right?
turns.zh: 我不会说参差不齐纯粹是我们的路线图。有些事模型确实很弱，这正是“品味”那套东西的用武之地，对吧？就像我说的，你能从这些模型里榨取出什么，这才是现实。我们叫它们系统一模型，原因之一——其实当初人们也不想让我们这么命名，因为系统一思维往往被当成坏事，人们拿它当贬义词用，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah. It's like the part that just naturally happened from evolution, from back in the day before —
turns.zh: 是啊。就像是进化中自然而然产生的那部分，从很久以前——

turns.en: Exactly. Instinctual, makes mistakes.
turns.zh: 没错。本能的，会犯错。

turns.en: Yeah. Exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊。没错。

turns.en: But people often say that is the mistake-making side, and I believe that the shape AI actually gets compressed to happens to be very system one. And therefore the honest thing to do is to communicate its weaknesses, because I think that on its own can be incredibly valuable for software. And most of what people need actually is system one stuff. Like, why can we solve millennium prize problems in math but not automate anything touching accounting? That should be really weird to a lot of people. And I think that is still our north star, even if people get distracted by cost, speed, oh it's good for really fast decisions or whatever else. I see these as distractions compared to what is really needed for AI to meet its potential. And that is my north star.
turns.zh: 但人们常说那是会犯错的一面，而我相信 AI 实际被压缩成的形态，恰好非常系统一。因此诚实的做法就是把它薄弱的地方讲清楚，因为我认为这本身对软件来说就极其宝贵。而人们真正需要的大部分东西，其实都是系统一那一类。比如，为什么我们能解决数学上的千禧年大奖难题，却没法自动化任何跟会计沾边的事？这在很多人看来应该非常奇怪。我认为这仍然是我们的北极星，即便人们被成本、速度、“它适合做快速决策”之类的东西分散了注意力。相比 AI 要发挥潜力真正需要的东西，我把这些看作干扰。而那就是我的北极星。

turns.en: So obviously you put the models out there and you have a lot of people using them in different ways. How much does the real-world usage of the models come and feed back into the roadmap versus just the stuff you all were planning to do?
turns.zh: 显然你们把模型放出去了，有很多人以不同方式使用它们。模型的真实使用情况有多少会反馈到路线图里，又有多少只是你们原本就计划要做的事？

turns.en: I would say it's almost none, real-world feedback. I think people should be complaining to us so much more. I think the field is still in a Stockholm syndrome of, oh yeah, the model providers just do stuff in their one-track path and we happen to be — like the victim is the wrong word, but — you know, like in that movie Wall-E, they're just like the people in the chairs just getting fed the AI. And I think this is the state of things right now, where people plan around AI changing but they don't have a sense of agency of where to take the field. And I think this is not the way it should go. That's actually really disempowering and kind of lame, in my opinion.
turns.zh: 我会说几乎没有，真实世界的反馈几乎没有。我觉得人们应该多得多地向我们抱怨。我觉得这个领域还处在一种斯德哥尔摩综合征里：哦对，模型厂商就沿着他们那条单行道做事，而我们恰好是——说“受害者”不太对，但——你知道，就像那部电影《机器人总动员》里，人们坐在椅子上，被喂着 AI。我觉得现在的情况就是这样：人们围绕 AI 的变化做规划，却没有一种“该把领域带向何方”的自主感。我认为这不该是发展方向。这其实非常让人无力，在我看来还挺逊的。

turns.en: And also, I think there's so much more we could do collaboratively as a field. I think the field could push us a lot more to say, hey, we want to be doing these things, we think it is within the realm of capabilities, let's figure out how to do it together — but not just putting stuff into the model, but figuring out how to prompt them, figuring out how to unlock capabilities. Let's work together for these sci-fi use cases, because I think that is the way the future is going to go. And I would want so much more of that.
turns.zh: 而且，我觉得作为一个领域，我们能协作做的事情多得多。我觉得这个领域可以更多地推动我们，说：嘿，我们想做这些事，我们认为这在能力范围之内，我们一起想办法做出来——不只是往模型里塞东西，而是研究怎么提示它们、怎么解锁能力。让我们一起把这些科幻般的用例做出来，因为我认为未来就会朝这个方向走。我会非常希望看到更多这样的东西。

turns.en: My joke internally is that the number one way to get me to respond to something is to talk about model jaggedness. Because you have very high-up people say, "Hey, can we meet with Diogo?" And I'm just like, "No, can you meet with my CTO or GTM head instead?" But if they complain about model intelligence, I am on that and debugging that myself, for better or for worse, because I think that is the thing that will really move the needle for us long term.
turns.zh: 我在内部开玩笑说，让我对某件事上心的头号办法，就是聊模型的参差不齐。因为会有级别很高的人说：“嘿，能跟 Diogo 见个面吗？”我就说：“不行，你能不能见见我的 CTO 或 GTM 负责人？”但如果他们抱怨模型的智能水平，我就会扑上去，亲自去调试，不管好坏，因为我认为那才是长期真正能推动我们前进的事。

turns.en: So right now we mostly have to go with our old roadmap, because we are not — I think people are still in that mode of, yes, let's just do whatever the model providers let us do, instead of let's collaborate on this insane future together.
turns.zh: 所以现在，我们大多只能按原来的路线图走，因为我们还没——我觉得人们还处在那种模式里：对，模型厂商让我们做什么我们就做什么，而不是一起协作去打造这个疯狂的未来。

turns.en: And actually there's another aspect of that. I think people have a deep distrust of model providers too, because they train on their data. And this whole discussion of can GPT wrappers even exist, I think is very disempowering too, because the whole application ends up becoming a chatbot. So the moat ends up becoming the equivalent of a system message that you send every time, versus the moat and the intelligence and the behavior and the specialization actually existing in software, where we just make little micro decisions for you and you do all of the sick logic.

I hope you make a decent amount of money, and I hope this enables other people to build all sorts of other things, because now this jaggedness thing is healed. And that is the relationship I hope to have. And this is why I'm so jazzed about software.
turns.zh: 我的理念是，我们应该让那些软件玩家在软件上赢。对，正是如此。但理想情况下，他们也告诉我们——我们不要他们的数据——但他们应该告诉我们，比如：嘿，你们在这个特定轴上有锯齿状的不稳定，让我们的东西变得不可靠，我们合作吧。其实他们可以直接告诉我们：我们完全不打算告诉你我们在做什么。这是这个任务的大致形状，修好它。而我会说：太棒了，非常感谢你告诉我们这些。希望它解决你的问题，也解决一大堆其他人的问题。我希望你在世界上产出大量价值。我希望你赚到相当多的钱，我希望这能让其他人构建各种各样的东西，因为这个锯齿状的问题被治好了。这就是我希望拥有的关系。这也是我为什么对软件如此兴奋。

transcript.sec: The tyranny of the KV cache

turns.en: No, I love it. You said something there that I wanted to come back to because it was just a great phrase. I think you said the tyranny of the KV cache in coding agents. Maybe explain for our listeners a little bit about some of the limitations in coding agents due to the KV cache, and how you think about that problem space.
turns.zh: 不，我很喜欢。你刚才说了一句话我想回头再聊，因为那是个很妙的说法。我记得你说的是编程智能体里“KV 缓存的暴政”。也许给听众解释一下，编程智能体因为 KV 缓存而受到的一些限制，以及你怎么看这个问题空间。

turns.en: I would say almost all design decisions around the UX of coding agents — the stuff that actually functionally changes stuff — is built around the KV cache. And this is natural, because the biggest wins in ML are always very hardware aware. This is how things have gotten so efficient recently, or pseudo-recently, since GPT-4's days. GPT-4 is very expensive, so you really need to design around this, which is great because it's efficient, but it's also quite limited.
turns.zh: 我会说，编程智能体用户体验的几乎所有设计决策——那些真正在功能上改变东西的部分——都是围绕 KV 缓存构建的。这很自然，因为机器学习里最大的收益总是非常硬件感知的。这就是最近、或者说伪最近、自 GPT-4 时代以来事情变得如此高效的原因。GPT-4 非常贵，所以你真的需要围绕这个来设计，这很好，因为它高效，但它也相当受限。

turns.en: This is why routing doesn't tend to work. Routing absolutely works if you're making the equivalent of what we call instruction-following calls — task in, task out, you know, throw the cache away. Routing is amazing for that. Actually, you can do way more advanced things than just routing in that case. There are so many advanced patterns you can do when that is your assumption. Like, you could actually try it with a cheap model, use an extremely cheap judge, and if it's efficient keep it, if not try a larger model, or try multiple times and pick the best. There are so many things you can do. But when you have this stateful KV cache, you are really constrained to it being kind of append-only, and you have this complicated trade-off, kind of like an IPython notebook where you can never delete from memory because it's like a really weird, you know, conglomerated state.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么路由往往行不通。如果你做的是我们所说的指令跟随调用——任务进、任务出，把缓存扔掉——路由绝对行得通。那种情况下路由非常棒。其实，在那种假设下，你能做比路由高级得多的事情。有太多高级模式可以做。比如，你其实可以用便宜模型试，用一个极便宜的评判器，如果高效就保留，不行就试更大的模型，或者试多次挑最好的。你能做太多事情。但当你有了这个有状态的 KV 缓存，你就真的被约束成只能追加，你面临一个复杂的权衡，有点像 IPython notebook，你永远不能从内存里删除，因为它是一个很奇怪的、 conglomerated 的状态。

turns.en: And it turns out it's very hard to engineer around this because the models are trained with it. So if you actually start doing fancy stateful operations with the models having free rein over that state, they'll end up looping and stuff like that, because they're so tuned to having that KV cache, so efficient to have a KV cache. So this prevents you from doing routing effectively. It prevents subagents from being really effective, because now you have this weird trade-off of what state, what context do I pass to my subagent, because this requires intelligence in order to know what to pass in. If you pass it all in, this is a huge input token cost instead of a cache read cost. And when your subagent makes an output, how do you know what to pass in? And what subset is relevant down the line? And the safest thing to do tends to be to append a lot of stuff.
turns.zh: 而事实证明，围绕这个做工程非常难，因为模型就是带着它训练的。所以如果你真的开始做花哨的有状态操作，让模型自由支配那个状态，它们最终会陷入循环之类的问题，因为它们太习惯于拥有那个 KV 缓存，拥有 KV 缓存太高效了。所以这阻止了你有效地做路由。它也阻止了子智能体真正有效，因为现在你面临一个奇怪的权衡：我该把什么状态、什么上下文传给子智能体，因为这需要智能才能知道该传什么。如果你全传进去，那就是巨大的输入 token 成本，而不是缓存读取成本。而当你的子智能体产出输出时，你怎么知道该传什么进去？哪些子集在后续是相关的？而最安全的做法往往是追加一大堆东西。

turns.en: And now this is the equivalent of, from a state management perspective, imagine your state is like global variables. It's passing one giant dictionary around forever until the models break and they start getting dumber over time because context rot is a real thing. And this is totally cool. Just to be clear, I don't believe there's anything super tragic about this on its own, because it's very useful. I think what's tragic is that it's really the only way to do it. And I think there are so many more advanced patterns that you could do if you could assume that I could just put intelligence all over these operations.
turns.zh: 这就相当于，从状态管理的角度，想象你的状态就像全局变量。它把一个巨大的字典永远传来传去，直到模型崩溃，它们开始随时间变笨，因为上下文腐化是真实存在的。这完全没问题。说清楚一点，我不认为这本身有什么特别悲剧的，因为它非常有用。我觉得悲剧的是，这真的是唯一做法。我认为如果你能假设我可以在这些操作上到处放智能，你能做太多更高级的模式。

turns.en: And that is the kind of thing to me that I think from a dis-engineering, architecture design, beauty, power perspective is so limiting. And that is what that tyranny is, because the people who have tried to do those cool algorithms have mostly failed because they've tried to use LLMs for it. And LLMs are not optimized for routing logic within the software or making discrete little decisions. They're optimized for making human-pleasing outputs that are not super reliable running as a subprocess. And this then makes people believe this doesn't work.
turns.zh: 对我来说，从逆向工程、架构设计、美感和力量的角度看，这种东西太受限了。这就是那种“暴政”，因为那些尝试做酷炫算法的人大多失败了，因为他们试图用 LLM 来做。而 LLM 并没有针对软件内部的路由逻辑或做出离散的小决策进行优化。它们优化的是生成讨人喜欢的输出，而这些输出作为子进程运行时并不太可靠。这就让人们相信这条路走不通。

turns.en: And actually a lot of what our original shape looks like is not too dissimilar from LangChain. Like there's nothing wrong with LangChain's interface, right? Some would even say that it was maybe perfect for classifiers on top of LLMs. I can't remember back in the day, but I'm pretty darn sure it's going to be pretty darn good if someone made a LangChain-compatible wrapper on top of our model. The problem is people didn't like it because it made models somewhat dumber, because the models are not optimized for that type of pattern.
turns.zh: 实际上，我们最初形态的很多地方和 LangChain 并没有太大不同。LangChain 的接口本身没什么问题，对吧？有些人甚至会说，它对于 LLM 之上的分类器来说可能堪称完美。我记不清当时的情况了，但我非常确定，如果有人在我们模型之上做一个兼容 LangChain 的封装，效果会相当不错。问题在于人们不喜欢它，因为它让模型变得有点笨，因为模型并没有针对那种模式进行优化。

turns.en: And this is also a form of tyranny, where everyone just thinks Anthropic and OpenAI or whoever else is number three right now is doing their best and giving us the best intelligence possible, when the reality is there are so many other intelligences possible. And there are trade-offs there. There are truly a lot of trade-offs that are made in this design that people can feel but cannot really measure, because it's really hard to do.
turns.zh: 这也是一种暴政：所有人都以为 Anthropic、OpenAI 或者现在排第三的那家已经在尽力，在给我们尽可能最好的智能。但现实是，还存在许多其他可能的智能形态。这里面有权衡。这个设计里确实做了大量权衡，人们能感觉到，却无法真正衡量，因为这真的很难做到。

transcript.sec: What a Coding Agent Could Look Like

turns.en: What's like an example of the shape of what a coding agent could look like, I guess with like a different intelligence design?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗，说明一个编码智能体在另一种智能设计下可能长什么样？

turns.en: One feature that I think would be really sick is, what if you could have multiple agents sharing the same context and truly reading and writing from the same context? That sounds really complicated. Like there's no way that works right now because of the KV cache, but nothing stops that from happening.
turns.zh: 我觉得会非常酷的一个功能是：如果能让多个智能体共享同一个上下文，真正从同一个上下文读写，会怎样？这听起来很复杂。因为 KV 缓存的原因，现在根本做不到，但没有什么能阻止它发生。

turns.en: And actually a very common pattern people have with agents these days is they're just clicking on crazy stuff. They don't know what's going on. And after it does the thing you asked it to do, people are like, make a visualizer or a dashboard or a learning tool. And it's kind of crazy that that has to be an extension of the context that has all of the trial and error in it, or starting from scratch looking at a git commit and rereading everything from scratch. Why can't it share the state?
turns.zh: 实际上，现在人们用智能体时一个非常常见的模式是，它们只是在乱点各种东西，根本不知道发生了什么。等它做完你让它做的事之后，人们就说：做一个可视化工具、仪表盘或者学习工具。而这件事竟然必须作为那个包含所有试错过程的上下文的延伸，或者从零开始看一个 git commit、从头重读一切，这有点疯狂。为什么它不能共享状态？

turns.en: And why can't you have an agent here that's basically read-only for the codebase but allows you to write the visualizer, such that as the agent is cooking you actually get live visualizations of what's going on—maybe using a slightly dumber model like Sonnet instead of Opus to write out what Opus is doing—so you get a sense of what's going on instead of having to read the jittery syncing updates or whatever else. I think that would be cool.
turns.zh: 为什么不能有一个智能体，对代码库基本是只读的，但允许你写可视化工具，这样当智能体在“烹饪”时，你实际上能实时看到正在发生什么——也许用一个稍微笨一点的模型，比如 Sonnet 而不是 Opus，来写出 Opus 正在做什么——这样你就能对情况有所感知，而不必去读那些抖动的同步更新之类的。我觉得那会很酷。

turns.en: Another example here is compaction. Compaction makes a lot of sense for a write-once, append-only KV cache, because it's full and we need to restart it. But compaction is a form of compression, and compression is just not totally solvable. It's very hard to compress without priors for compression. But what happens if you compress based on what problem you were solving before, and now you want to ask a problem that is different from that one, and it would use information that was compressed away? That agent is very much losing hand.
turns.zh: 另一个例子是压缩（compaction）。对于一次写入、只追加的 KV 缓存来说，压缩很合理，因为它满了，我们需要重启。但压缩是一种压缩形式，而压缩并不是完全可解的。在没有压缩先验的情况下，压缩非常困难。但如果你基于之前正在解决的问题进行压缩，而现在你想问一个不同的问题，而这个问题会用到被压缩掉的信息，会怎样？那个智能体就非常吃亏了。

turns.en: But what if how the state gets compressed was actually semantic, and it could detect, hey, I'm doing a new task, I should actually think about what the context should be for this new task using an ROI calculation, which should be in code. The code should compute the expected value of cache reads and cache writes and everything, and recalculate perhaps a new KV cache for this other task, and maybe even keep the other one hot. I don't really know. This sounds like cool sci-fi.
turns.zh: 但如果状态的压缩方式实际上是语义化的，它能检测到：嘿，我在做一个新任务，我应该用 ROI 计算来思考这个新任务的上下文应该是什么，而这个计算应该写在代码里。代码应该计算缓存读取和缓存写入等的期望值，也许为这个新任务重新计算一个新的 KV 缓存，甚至可能让另一个缓存保持热状态。我不太确定。这听起来像很酷的科幻。

turns.en: One more, but then I will stop on this topic. I just got excited about this. One thing that I think would be really cool is, hey, I keep cooking on the same codebase and I keep reading the same files and having to re-understand my system's abstractions over and over and over again. There's a partial solution to this, which is maybe the agent should write markdown files, but then how do you keep it in sync? It's kind of a pain.
turns.zh: 再说一个，然后我就不在这个话题上继续了。我只是对这个很兴奋。我觉得会非常酷的一件事是：嘿，我一直在同一个代码库上“烹饪”，我一直在读同样的文件，不得不一遍又一遍地重新理解我系统的抽象。这有一个部分解决方案，也许智能体应该写 markdown 文件，但然后你怎么保持同步？这有点烦。

turns.en: But what if you could look at the history of old models—not as a hack, like right now it's a little bit of a hack: oh, it's a tool that you can use sometimes if the model deems it necessary—but what if by its nature one of the first steps you do is even an extremely cheap map over the overall history to find the relevant stuff here? And what if that history could also be shared with your co-workers who are using the same codebase, so you can actually have insights from what they're working on? These are very doable software problems, right? The problem is it's very unfriendly with a KV cache when all the intelligence needs to be append-only. And there are so many other cool things.
turns.zh: 但如果你能查看旧模型的历史——不是作为一种 hack，现在它有点像个 hack：哦，这是一个工具，如果模型认为有必要，有时可以用——但如果它的本质是，你做的第一步之一甚至是对整体历史做一个极其廉价的 map，来找到这里相关的东西，会怎样？如果那段历史还能与使用同一代码库的同事共享，这样你实际上能从他们正在做的工作中获得洞见，会怎样？这些都是非常可行的软件问题，对吧？问题在于，当所有智能都需要是只追加的时候，这对 KV 缓存非常不友好。还有很多其他酷炫的东西。

turns.zh: 对，各方面都是，尤其是算力。据我所闻，金融工程是他们最大的优势，而我完全不知道那里面有多盘根错节，也不知道市场往任何方向走时他们会有多脆弱。你知道，泡沫可以仅仅因为预期没兑现就破掉，而不是因为它不是真正具有变革性的技术。所以我尽量让自己的预测保持校准。在没有内部信息时，我尽量不过度自信，我是个比较保守的人。我感觉很多被计入的预期不只是产品层面的，而是基于对 AI 未来及其能力的误解。所以我猜，因为有些人可能把它估成“造神基本等于无限”，那里会有一定程度的错配。而我觉得“让他们治愈癌症”会变成玛丽·安托瓦内特的“让他们吃蛋糕”。

turns.en: That is a good line.
turns.zh: 这句话说得好。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, obviously—
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，显然——

turns.en: Oh, maybe it did end spicy then.
turns.zh: 哦，那也许结尾确实挺辣的。

turns.en: That was a great line. Yeah. I mean, obviously so many people are underwriting the move from coding agents to general knowledge work to bio to these other spaces, and obviously not the perfect use cases for RLVR by any means. I still get the sense that the nuanced way to understand agents — perhaps and maybe all of AI right now — is what decisions can you trust them with in terms of stakes for the company, and can you get value without too much of the downside. And coding is quite unique in this, or math is actually super-duper unique, where there's no downside other than the compute you spend, right? Math models do not cost companies anything except if they're paying people to validate their proofs, which it's unclear if they even pay them for that.
turns.zh: 那句话很棒。是啊。我是说，显然有很多人在押注从编程智能体到通用知识工作、到生物、再到其他这些领域的迁移，而且显然这些绝不是 RLVR 的完美用例。我仍然觉得，理解智能体——也许还有当下所有 AI——的细腻方式，是看在公司风险层面你能把哪些决策托付给它们，以及你能不能在不承担太多下行风险的情况下获得价值。编程在这方面相当独特，或者数学其实超级独特，因为除了你花的算力，没有下行风险，对吧？数学模型不会让公司付出任何代价，除非他们付钱让人验证证明，而他们到底付不付钱都不清楚。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: To me — maybe someone knows. But code also has somewhat more kept downside because you have a git, right? And you have humans in the loop, and there are ways to protect you from unwanted side effects, which is the main downside of powerful tools. And powerful tools are necessary to do knowledge work because knowledge work often involves side effects in the world. I'm talking a lot like a computer scientist right now. My sense is that for a lot of other fields, they don't have anywhere close to the same levels of safeguards and ability to revert and tracking and all of that. And that is why, to my knowledge, no one has automated a drive-thru yet, even though people have tried really, really hard — and the stakes of a drive-thru are a lot lower than the stakes of many other forms of knowledge work. So I think the truth will be that there'll be nuance and skill into it, and the people who will be the big winners are not the ones who just YOLO all in, but those who understand reality and deploy them in line with the realities of technology. So I'm not — given my state of AI — I feel like most people are very FOMO-driven and they do not have a great understanding of the state of AI, and they will probably err on the overoptimistic, which will get them burned with many side effects, or over-pessimistic, which is business as usual, which is how most businesses have been for this AI boom.
turns.zh: 对我来说——也许有人知道。但代码的下行风险也多少更可控一些，因为你有 git，对吧？你有回路中的人类，有办法保护你免受不想要的副作用，而副作用正是强大工具的主要缺点。而强大工具是做知识工作所必需的，因为知识工作往往涉及现实世界中的副作用。我现在说话很像计算机科学家。我的感觉是，很多其他领域根本没有接近同等水平的防护措施、回滚能力、追踪等等。这就是为什么据我所知，还没有人把得来速自动化，尽管人们非常非常努力地尝试过——而来得速的风险比许多其他形式的知识工作低得多。所以我认为真相会是：这里面需要细腻和技巧，而大赢家不会是那些直接梭哈的人，而是理解现实、并按照技术现实去部署它们的人。所以，鉴于我对 AI 现状的判断，我觉得大多数人非常受 FOMO 驱动，对 AI 现状没有很好的理解，他们很可能会偏向过度乐观，从而被许多副作用烧伤；或者偏向过度悲观，那就是照旧，也就是大多数企业在这次 AI 热潮中的样子。

turns.en: One thing you said there — I'm curious, you said you have an estimate for how much these coding agents actually improve engineering productivity. What is that estimate?
turns.zh: 你刚才说到一件事——我很好奇，你说你对这些编程智能体实际提升工程生产力有多少有个估计。那个估计是多少？

turns.en: Okay, I will say I have error bars on this because I think there are long-term effects like skill degradation and tech debt and stuff like this. So my estimates are in the 20 to 40% speed-up range, but again it really depends on the use case, and it also depends on the skill of the user. And if you can — because the side effects are the bad thing — if you can isolate the side effects in a way that those are very legible.
turns.zh: 好，我得说这有误差范围，因为我认为存在长期效应，比如技能退化、技术债之类。所以我的估计是在 20% 到 40% 的提速区间，但同样，这真的取决于用例，也取决于用户的技能水平。而且如果你能——因为副作用才是坏东西——如果你能把副作用隔离到非常清晰可辨的程度。

turns.en: So depending on the use case, for some it's kind of like an infinite percent speed up. You know, you would do things you could never do otherwise. For others, they are just so bad that they're as bad as coding the thing by hand. I would guess on average it's like a decent but small boost. And I believe that is the consensus that I've seen in the field right now.
turns.zh: 所以取决于使用场景，对某些场景来说，这几乎是无限倍的加速。你知道，你可以做以前永远做不到的事情。对其他场景来说，它们太糟糕了，糟糕到跟手工写代码差不多。我猜平均来说，这是一个不错但小幅的提升。我相信这就是我目前在领域内看到的共识。

turns.en: Yeah. Another question I'm not totally sure how you answer, like, how can you know? There's obviously so much discourse around AI safety these days. Like, how concerned are you about a lot of these, you know, this AI safety conversation?
turns.zh: 是的。另一个问题，我不太确定你怎么回答，比如你怎么知道？显然现在关于 AI 安全的讨论非常多。比如，你对这些 AI 安全对话有多担心？

turns.en: I think AI safety is not one monolith and there's like a ton of different slices of it. I think that the ASI discussion is actually extremely different from the biorisk discussion, which is very different from like the cyber risk discussion, which is different than like trust in trust and safety.
turns.zh: 我认为 AI 安全不是一个单一的整体，它有很多不同的切片。我觉得 ASI 的讨论实际上与生物风险的讨论截然不同，而生物风险又与网络风险的讨论非常不同，网络风险又不同于信任与安全。

turns.en: Maybe like ASI versus like bad actors, you know, using bio and cyber and whatnot.
turns.zh: 也许比如 ASI 与恶意行为者，你知道，利用生物和网络等等。

turns.en: I get the sense that most people concerned with ASI are a little bit divorced from the reality of the technology and this has been the case since day one. You know, like, I feel like you need to actually build a reliable system with AI to have a voice in the room that something's going to be so reliably, maybe not evil but misaligned that it can destroy the world. But I think we're pretty far from stuff like that. Additionally, there's actually a bunch of nuance towards like, you know, ASI, RSI, and like whether or not the models have a sense of agency on their own. Like paperclip maximizer is actually very different than bad actor programs super employee to destroy the world type things. And actually, I think that those end up becoming quite different in threat model. I think that we're breakthroughs away from true agency. As much as people like to read these chains of thought and try to ascribe real agency to it, I would guess that we are something like two breakthroughs of gigantic magnitude away from this. I think even one breakthrough would not be sufficient is my guess, but maybe one gigantic one could be. And I think the threat model of like humans with super tools who want to do damage is very different than the ASI RSI thing. I don't, I think a lot of people who also believe in RSI both have not studied the history of AI very much and also have no appreciation of Andal's law. Where like, you know, if you assume that intelligence is the spectrum and it's the only one that matters and you have to map things into that spectrum and you can also map humans and chimpanzees. It's a horrible argument in my opinion. Then it does look bad but the reality is that it doesn't work that way and like the nuance of the many different types of intelligence and how to do them reliably matters a lot in this whole analogy. Could the field of AI development become a little bit faster? Yes, but people have been trying this for a long time and it usually doesn't work out and I don't think that people would count like a 10% speed up on AI research as RSI if it doesn't actually increase over time. So I'm very open to being convinced by evidence, but I think that it's more of a philosophical problem rather than a technological one. The kinds of people who like read a Boston super intelligence and treat it like reality over a very interesting sci-fi book makes me kind of worried.
turns.zh: 我感觉大多数关心 ASI 的人有点脱离技术的现实，而且从一开始就是这样。你知道，我觉得你需要真正用 AI 构建一个可靠的系统，才能在房间里有一席之地，说某个东西会如此可靠地——也许不是邪恶，而是对齐失败——以至于它能毁灭世界。但我认为我们离那种东西还很远。此外，关于 ASI、RSI 以及模型本身是否有自主意识，其实有很多细微差别。比如回形针最大化器实际上与恶意行为者程序超级员工毁灭世界之类的事情非常不同。实际上，我认为这些在威胁模型上最终会变得相当不同。我认为我们距离真正的自主性还差几个突破。尽管人们喜欢解读这些思维链并试图赋予它真正的自主性，但我猜我们距离这个目标还差大约两个巨大规模的突破。我猜甚至一个突破都不够，但也许一个巨大的突破可能就够了。而且我认为，拥有超级工具并想造成破坏的人类，其威胁模型与 ASI、RSI 的事情非常不同。我不——我认为很多相信 RSI 的人既没有研究过多少 AI 历史，也不了解安达尔定律。比如，你知道，如果你假设智能是一个光谱，而且是唯一重要的东西，你必须把事物映射到那个光谱中，你也可以把人类和黑猩猩映射进去。在我看来这是一个糟糕的论点。然后它看起来确实很糟，但现实是它并不是那样运作的，而许多不同类型的智能以及如何可靠地实现它们的细微差别在这个整个类比中非常重要。AI 开发领域能变得快一点吗？是的，但人们已经尝试这个很久了，通常并不成功，而且我不认为人们会把 AI 研究上 10% 的加速算作 RSI，如果它实际上并没有随时间增加的话。所以我非常愿意被证据说服，但我认为这更像是一个哲学问题而不是技术问题。那些喜欢读波士顿超级智能并把它当作现实而不是一本非常有趣的科幻书的人，让我有点担心。
